english.html: in whose first youth the desire of the flesh once boiled up so much that one, at about nine years, got his wet-nurse with child g; and another, having scarcely reached his tenth, provoked by the immodest and lascivious acts of his mistress (who made him lie with her), knew her at last and made her pregnant h. And again of a little girl who, at about nine years, bore a child i. Which also, or very nearly, several attribute to the kings Solomon and Ahaz, who (according to the reckoning that some make) had children between ten and eleven years of age k: for Solomon had Rehoboam, and Ahaz had Hezekiah l. But what of it? Although for the one child (Saint Jerome, for greater assurance, calls the Lord to witness that he does not lie) THE LORD BEING MY WITNESS, he says, I DO NOT LIE (Domino teste, non mentior) m, and the other authors are likewise men of great learning and commendable good faith: nevertheless their authority is not necessary, nor so venerable, that the reader should be obliged to believe them n. And as for Solomon and Ahaz, many very learned writers reckon their years otherwise. Be that as it may, even if it were so, these are fine examples, certainly, and memorable: but so rare, nonetheless, that we neither ought nor can make a precedent of them o. And our laws in this matter, as in all others, fix upon the cases and affairs which they see or think most often to happen p. Indeed, that great oracle of Philosophy, Plato, speaking of the age suitable for men and women to marry, prescribed for men the thirtieth year, up to the thirty-fifth: and for women, from the sixteenth up to the twentieth q; and Aristotle his disciple, the thirty-sixth for males, and the eighteenth for females r. True it is that in this our legislators have, far more prudently as it seems to me, foreseen and considered that many are so ill-born, and of a concupiscence so immoderately forward, that if by means of the nuptial union they could not extinguish the ardour that begins to inflame and prick them, they might brutally throw themselves into filthy and detestable lusts. For which reason they have made the use of marriage somewhat earlier, and freer, than Plato or Aristotle: namely, in the fourteenth year for the man, and in the twelfth for the wo

notes.citation: Glossa ordinaria on the Decretum, in the summa to C. 20 q. 1; Johannes Andreae and Panormitanus (Iean André & Panorme) on c. Puberes, X 4.2 (De desponsatione impuberum); all citing Gregory the Great, Dialogues
notes.original: Gloſe en la ſomme xx. q. i. Iean André & Panorme au c. puberes, de deſponſ. impub. tous alleguans S. Gregoire en ſes dialogues.
notes.gloss: The example of the boy of nine who got his nurse with child; the chapter number of Puberes and the locus in the Dialogues have not been verified.

notes.original: S. Hierome en vne de ſes epiſtres adreſſee ad Vitalem.
notes.gloss: Jerome answers Vitalis's question whether Solomon and Ahaz begot sons at eleven, and tells of a boy of ten, reared by a woman who made him sleep with her, who got her pregnant.

notes.citation: Albericus de Rosate (Alberique), Dictionarium iuris, s.v. Matrimonium, second entry
notes.original: Alberique, en ſon dictionnaire, ſur la diction Matrimoniũ 2.

notes.citation: Johannes Andreae and Panormitanus on the last chapter of Decretals X 4.13 (De eo qui cognovit consanguineam uxoris suae vel sponsae)
notes.original: Io. And. & Panor. au c. fin. de eo qui dux. cõſ. vxo. aux Decret.
notes.gloss: Coras's dux. is a misprint for cog.: annot-002 note {l} cites the same title as de eo qui cog. cons. vxo. Cited for the computation of Solomon's and Ahaz's ages; chapter number not verified.

notes.original: Au liu. 3. des Rois c. xi. & au 4. cha. xviii.
notes.gloss: Solomon's forty-year reign and Rehoboam's accession at forty-one; Hezekiah's accession at twenty-five after Ahaz's sixteen-year reign begun at twenty, whence the reckoning that each father was about eleven at his son's birth.
The words Domino teste, non mentior, vouching for the boy of ten.

notes.citation: Decretals, X 3.10 (De his quae fiunt a praelato sine consensu capituli), c. Cum apostolica; Decretum Gratiani D. 9, c. Ego solis (cf. D. 9 c. 5)
notes.original: c. cum apoſtolica. de iis que ſi. à præ. aux Decretal. c. ego ſolis, en la diſtinction ix du Decret.
notes.gloss: Augustine: only the canonical Scriptures command unconditional belief; other authors, however holy and learned, may be doubted. The chapter number of Cum apostolica has not been verified.

notes.citation: Decretum Gratiani D. 61, c. Statuimus, last paragraph
notes.original: c. ſtatuimus. Paragt. dernier lxi. diſtinction.
notes.gloss: Chapter number not verified; cited for the rule that rare cases are no precedent.

notes.original: L. nam ad ea. D, de legi.
notes.gloss: Celsus: "the law ought rather to be adapted to what happens frequently and easily than to what happens very rarely."

notes.original: Platon au 6. liure de ſa Republique, & au vi. des loix.
notes.gloss: Coras writes "the sixth book of the Republic"; the ages are in book 5. The Laws give thirty to thirty-five for men and sixteen to twenty for women, the figures Coras quotes.
Aristotle: about eighteen for women and thirty-seven "or a little less" for men; Coras's thirty-six.

the final a is heavily inked and carries a short slanted stroke above it that could be read as a tilde ('lã'); 'Gloſe en la ſomme' is the sense, so it is read as a plain a with a stray mark. The line does end there — there is clear white space to its right.
the mark between 'xx' and 'q.' is set high and looks like a short dash rather than a point; read as the full stop the citation form requires (xx. q. i.).
a small dot sits between 'ſon' and 'diction'; much smaller than the note's commas and full stops, so taken as a speck. The word ends in a full n (the next line begins 'naire'), not a tilde.

the note's key letter is an italic k — a looped ascender plus a z-shaped leg — which at reading size looks like the two letters 'lz'. Read as key k, matching the {k} marker in the body. The first letter of 'Io.' is drawn with the same loop as the italic l, so the line could be read 'lo. And.'; 'Io. And. & Panor.' (Ioannes Andreae and Panormitanus) is the sense.
a small raised tick is printed between 'Panor.' and 'au'; transcribed as an apostrophe. It may be a broken sort or an offset mark.

the middle of the first word shows two strokes carrying what look like one or two dots, so it could be read 'diix.' or 'diux.'; 'dux.' (de eo qui duxit) is the reading taken. The ſ of 'cõſ.' is a long s.

the last letter has a closed bowl and reads as e, giving 'eſcriuane'; the sense wants 'eſcriuant' (S. Hierome eſcriuant ad Vitalem), so this may be a misprint or an inked-in italic t. Transcribed as read.
the letter before the stop is read as the æ ligature (à præ[lato]); at this size it could be a plain a.
the last letter before the stop has a tall crossed ascender: the italic t, not the short italic r. Read 'Paragt.' (sic for 'Paragr.'); reader A read 'Paragr.'
the mark after the swash italic D has a tail below the baseline and is read as a comma, unlike the plain round point after 'ea.' beside it; it could be a full stop.
the last line of note q ('& au vi. des' / 'loix.') is printed at the start of the foot block, before note r, because the margin ran out at the foot of the column; merged into note q as one note.
the gathering mark is printed 'A ij.' with a full stop after the j; kept as printed (p001 carries a bare 'A').
